fields.Text: In the relational model, a table is called a {{c1::relation}}, a row a tuple, and a column an attribute.
fields.Hint: Codd borrowed the word from set theory.
fields.Fact: Codd defined relations as sets, so in theory a relation has no duplicate tuples and no row order.
fields.Source: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks, E. F. Codd, 1970 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362384.362685)

fields.Question: In what year did E. F. Codd publish "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks"?
fields.Hint: The very start of a decade.
fields.Fact: Codd wrote the paper while working at IBM, and it appeared in Communications of the ACM.
fields.Source: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks, E. F. Codd, 1970 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362384.362685)

fields.Text: A {{c1::primary key}} is a chosen candidate key that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.
fields.Hint: Every table should usually have exactly one of these.
fields.Fact: A table can have several candidate keys, but only one is designated primary.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: SELECT (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html)
A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks, E. F. Codd, 1970 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362384.362685)

fields.Text: A {{c1::foreign key}} is a column set whose values must match a key in another (or the same) table, enforcing referential integrity.
fields.Fact: A foreign key can reference its own table, which is a common way to model hierarchies like managers.

fields.Question: Which join returns only rows that have a match in both tables?
fields.Hint: It is what plain JOIN means.
fields.Fact: In SQL, JOIN with no qualifier is an inner join.

fields.Question: Which join keeps every row from the first table and fills unmatched columns from the second with NULL?
fields.Hint: Think about which side is preserved.
fields.Fact: A LEFT JOIN followed by WHERE right.col IS NULL is a classic way to find rows with no match.

fields.Question: Which join keeps unmatched rows from both tables, padding the missing side with NULLs?
fields.Fact: MySQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN directly; it is usually emulated with a UNION of left and right joins.

fields.Question: Which join produces the Cartesian product of two tables?
fields.Hint: Every row pairs with every row.
fields.Fact: A cross join of a 1,000 row table with itself yields 1,000,000 rows.

fields.Text: WHERE EXISTS (subquery) expresses a {{c1::semi join}}: each outer row is returned at most once if any match exists.
fields.Hint: The opposite with NOT EXISTS has a related name.
fields.Fact: Unlike an inner join, a semi join never duplicates outer rows when there are several matches.

fields.Text: WHERE NOT EXISTS (subquery) expresses an {{c1::anti join}}: rows with no match on the other side.
fields.Hint: The negated cousin of a semi join.
fields.Fact: NOT EXISTS is usually safer than NOT IN, because NOT IN behaves surprisingly when the subquery returns NULL.

fields.Question: If the subquery in x NOT IN (subquery) returns a NULL and no match is found, what does the predicate evaluate to?
fields.Fact: Because the result is never true, the outer query returns no rows for such x.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Subquery Expressions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Comparison Functions and Operators (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-comparison.html)

fields.Question: What does NULL = NULL evaluate to in standard SQL?
fields.Fact: Use IS NULL, or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, to compare values that may be NULL.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Comparison Functions and Operators (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-comparison.html)

fields.Question: Which counts rows including those where col is NULL: COUNT(*) or COUNT(col)?
fields.Fact: Most aggregates, such as SUM and AVG, also ignore NULL inputs.

fields.Question: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
fields.Hint: WHERE runs too early for this.
fields.Fact: HAVING can reference aggregates like COUNT(*), which WHERE cannot.

fields.Question: In logical query processing, which clause is evaluated first: FROM, WHERE, SELECT or ORDER BY?
fields.Hint: You need rows before you can filter them.
fields.Fact: This is why a column alias defined in SELECT is not visible in WHERE.

fields.Question: Can a column alias defined in the SELECT list be referenced in the WHERE clause of the same query in standard SQL?
fields.Fact: ORDER BY can use SELECT aliases because it is logically evaluated after SELECT.

fields.Question: Which operator combines two result sets without removing duplicates?
fields.Fact: UNION ALL is usually cheaper because it skips the deduplication step.

fields.Question: Which standard SQL set operator returns rows from the first query that are not in the second?
fields.Fact: Like UNION, EXCEPT removes duplicates unless written as EXCEPT ALL.

fields.Text: A {{c1::window function}} computes a value across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them into one output row.
fields.Fact: PostgreSQL added window functions in version 8.4.

fields.Question: Inside an OVER clause, which two words split rows into independent groups for the window function?
fields.Hint: Similar in spirit to GROUP BY but rows are kept.
fields.Fact: Without it, the whole result set is one partition.

fields.Question: Which ranking function leaves gaps after ties, giving 1, 1, 3?
fields.Hint: One of its siblings does not leave gaps.
fields.Fact: RANK equals one plus the number of rows that sort strictly before the current row.

fields.Question: Which ranking function gives ties the same rank with no gaps, producing 1, 1, 2?
fields.Hint: Its name says the ranks are packed.
fields.Fact: DENSE_RANK counts distinct peer groups rather than rows.

fields.Question: Which window function assigns a unique sequential integer to each row in a partition, even for ties?
fields.Hint: Ties get broken arbitrarily unless ORDER BY is fully determined.
fields.Fact: A common use is picking the latest row per group with WHERE rn = 1 in an outer query.

fields.Question: Which window function returns a value from a previous row in the partition?
fields.Fact: LAG accepts an offset and a default value used when no such row exists.

fields.Text: When a window has ORDER BY but no frame clause, the default frame is {{c1::RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW}}.
fields.Extra: This makes SUM produce a running total that includes all peers of the current row.
fields.Hint: Running totals come from this default.
fields.Fact: Because it is RANGE, tied rows share the same running total.

fields.Text:
SELECT day, amount,
  {{c1::SUM(amount)}} OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running_total
FROM sales;
fields.Extra: The default frame accumulates from the first row to the current row.
fields.Fact: Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY, so they cannot be filtered in the same query level.

fields.Text: A {{c1::common table expression}} is a named subquery defined with WITH and referenced in the main statement.
fields.Hint: It reads like a temporary named view.
fields.Fact: CTEs can also wrap INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements in PostgreSQL.

fields.Text:
WITH {{c1::RECURSIVE}} t(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM t WHERE n < 5
)
SELECT n FROM t;
fields.Hint: The keyword that lets a CTE refer to itself.
fields.Fact: A recursive CTE has a non recursive term, then UNION or UNION ALL, then the recursive term.
DDL statements are transactional in PostgreSQL, so a failed migration can be rolled back.
SELECT is often grouped with DML, though some texts list it separately as DQL.
Recursive CTEs became part of standard SQL in SQL:1999.

fields.Text:
INSERT INTO counters (id, n) VALUES (1, 1)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO {{c1::UPDATE SET n = counters.n + 1}};
fields.Hint: The action that changes the existing row.
fields.Fact: The proposed row is available as EXCLUDED inside the DO UPDATE clause.

fields.Text: PostgreSQL's {{c1::RETURNING}} clause makes INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE return the affected rows.
fields.Hint: Saves a second round trip to read generated ids.
fields.Fact: SQLite also supports RETURNING since version 3.35.0.

fields.Text: {{c1::First normal form}} requires every attribute to hold a single atomic value, with no repeating groups.
fields.Fact: What counts as atomic is debated; arrays and JSON columns blur the line.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: {{c1::Second normal form}} requires 1NF and that no non key attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key.
fields.Hint: Only relevant when keys have more than one column.
fields.Fact: A 1NF table whose candidate keys are all single columns is automatically in 2NF.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: {{c1::Third normal form}} requires 2NF and that no non key attribute depends transitively on a key through another non key attribute.
fields.Hint: Watch out for a column that determines another column.
fields.Fact: Storing both zip code and city can violate it if zip code determines city.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: In {{c1::Boyce Codd normal form}}, the left side of every nontrivial functional dependency is a superkey.
fields.Fact: Every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: {{c1::Fourth normal form}} removes nontrivial multivalued dependencies that are not implied by a key.
fields.Hint: Two independent lists stored in one table.
fields.Fact: Kent's example: an employee's skills and languages stored in one table create spurious combinations.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: {{c1::Fifth normal form}} deals with join dependencies: a table that can be losslessly rebuilt only by joining three or more projections.
fields.Hint: It concerns tables rebuilt from three or more pieces.
fields.Fact: Fifth normal form is also known as project join normal form.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Fact: Raymond Boyce and Edgar Codd described it in 1974.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: The mnemonic for 3NF says every non key attribute must depend on "the key, {{c1::the whole key}}, and {{c2::nothing but the key}}".
fields.Fact: The middle part corresponds to 2NF and the last part to 3NF.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: A {{c1::functional dependency}} X → Y holds when any two rows that agree on X must also agree on Y.
fields.Hint: The basis of all normal form definitions up to BCNF.
fields.Fact: A key is exactly a set of attributes that functionally determines every attribute.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: Storing the same fact in many rows risks an {{c1::update anomaly}}, where changing one copy leaves others inconsistent.
fields.Hint: One of three classic anomalies normalization prevents.
fields.Fact: The other two classic ones are insertion and deletion anomalies.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: A {{c1::deletion anomaly}} occurs when removing a row unintentionally loses an unrelated fact stored only in that row.
fields.Hint: Deleting the last student of a course loses the course.
fields.Fact: Splitting the table so each fact lives in one place removes it.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: {{c1::Denormalization}} deliberately reintroduces redundancy, trading write complexity for faster reads.
fields.Hint: Common in reporting and analytics schemas.
fields.Fact: Star schemas in data warehouses are intentionally denormalized dimension tables around fact tables.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Question: Which normal form specifically targets transitive dependencies on the key?
fields.Hint: One step after removing partial dependencies.
fields.Fact: Codd defined 1NF, 2NF and 3NF in the early 1970s.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Question: Which normal form specifically targets partial dependencies on a composite key?
fields.Hint: It only matters for multi column keys.
fields.Fact: 2NF is defined relative to every candidate key, not just the primary key.
fields.Source: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory, William Kent, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/358024.358054)

fields.Text: A {{c1::B-tree}} index keeps keys sorted in a balanced tree, supporting equality, range queries and ordered scans.
fields.Hint: The default index type almost everywhere.
fields.Fact: Bayer and McCreight described B-trees in 1970 while at Boeing Research Labs; the journal paper followed in 1972.
fields.Source:
Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes, R. Bayer and E. McCreight, 1972 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00288683)
PostgreSQL Documentation: Index Types (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html)

fields.Question: What index type does PostgreSQL create when CREATE INDEX specifies no method?
fields.Fact: B-tree is the only built in PostgreSQL index type that can back a UNIQUE constraint.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL index type supports only equality comparisons?
fields.Fact: PostgreSQL hash indexes have been WAL logged and crash safe since version 10.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL index type is designed for values containing many elements, such as arrays, jsonb and full text?
fields.Fact: GIN stands for Generalized Inverted Index.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL index framework underlies most geometric and range type indexing, including PostGIS?
fields.Fact: GiST supports nearest neighbor ordering searches for some operator classes.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL index stores summaries per block range, staying tiny on huge naturally ordered tables?
fields.Hint: Great for append only timestamp data.
fields.Fact: A BRIN index can be orders of magnitude smaller than a B-tree on the same column.
BRIN was added in PostgreSQL 9.5.
The default full text indexing choice in PostgreSQL.

fields.Text: A {{c1::covering index}} contains every column a query needs, so the query can be answered from the index alone.
fields.Hint: The table itself need not be read.
fields.Fact: In PostgreSQL 11 and later, INCLUDE adds non key payload columns to a B-tree for this purpose.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-index-only-scans.html)

fields.Text: In PostgreSQL an {{c1::index-only scan}} still consults the visibility map, and visits the heap for pages not marked all visible.
fields.Fact: On a freshly bulk loaded table that has not been vacuumed, index-only scans may still fetch most heap pages.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-index-only-scans.html)

fields.Question: A B-tree index on (a, b) is most useful for queries that constrain which column?
fields.Aliases:
leading column
the leading column
first column
fields.Hint: Order of columns in the index matters.
fields.Fact: Equality on the leading columns plus a range on the next one is the most efficient pattern.

fields.Text: A composite B-tree index can serve queries that filter on a {{c1::leftmost prefix}} of its columns.
fields.Hint: Phone books sort by surname, then first name.
fields.Fact: This is why column order in a composite index should follow your most common filters.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL Documentation: Multicolumn Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)
SQLite: Query Planning (https://www.sqlite.org/queryplanner.html)

fields.Text:
CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at)
  {{c1::WHERE status = 'open'}};
fields.Extra: Only rows matching the predicate are indexed.
fields.Hint: This clause makes it a partial index.
fields.Fact: Partial unique indexes can enforce uniqueness only among a subset of rows.

fields.Text: CREATE INDEX ON users ({{c1::lower(email)}});
fields.Extra: Lets WHERE lower(email) = ... use an index.
fields.Hint: An index on an expression rather than a column.
fields.Fact: The query must use the same expression for the planner to match the index.

fields.Text: PostgreSQL's CREATE INDEX {{c1::CONCURRENTLY}} builds an index without blocking writes on the table.
fields.Fact: It cannot run inside a transaction block and takes longer than a normal build.

fields.Text: In MySQL's InnoDB, table rows are stored in the {{c1::clustered index}}, which is ordered by the primary key.
fields.Extra: Secondary indexes store the primary key value to find the row.
fields.Fact: A long primary key in InnoDB makes every secondary index larger.
fields.Source: MySQL Reference Manual: Clustered and Secondary Indexes (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-index-types.html)

fields.Text: An index is most useful when the predicate is highly {{c1::selective}}, matching a small fraction of rows.
fields.Hint: A boolean column with 50 percent true is a poor candidate.
fields.Fact: Planners often prefer a sequential scan when a large share of the table matches.

fields.Text: A predicate is {{c1::sargable}} when it can use an index to narrow the search, such as col >= 10 rather than col + 1 >= 11.
fields.Hint: Wrapping the column in arithmetic or a function often breaks this.
fields.Fact: The term comes from "search argument" in early IBM System R work.
fields.Source: Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System, Selinger et al., 1979 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/582095.582099)

fields.Question: In PostgreSQL, which command shows the plan along with actual run times and row counts?
fields.Fact: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the statement, so wrap data changing statements in a transaction you roll back.

fields.Question: Does EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an UPDATE actually modify rows?
fields.Fact: The PostgreSQL docs suggest BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK; to avoid side effects.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL command collects table statistics that the planner uses for estimates?
fields.Fact: Statistics include most common values and histograms per column.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: Statistics Used by the Planner (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-stats.html)

fields.Question: What is the PostgreSQL plan node that reads every row of a table in physical order?
fields.Fact: For small tables or low selectivity filters, it is often the cheapest plan.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL scan builds a bitmap of matching pages from an index, then reads those pages in physical order?
fields.Hint: It sits between index scans and sequential scans.
fields.Fact: Bitmaps from several indexes can be combined with AND or OR.

fields.Question: Which join algorithm builds an in memory table from the smaller input, then probes it with the other?
fields.Fact: Hash joins only work for equality join conditions.

fields.Question: Which join algorithm walks two inputs sorted on the join key side by side?
fields.Fact: An index that already provides the order can avoid an explicit sort step.

fields.Question: Which join algorithm scans the inner input once for every outer row, and is good when the outer side is tiny?
fields.Hint: The simplest of the three PostgreSQL join methods.
fields.Fact: With an index on the inner side, a nested loop join can be very fast for few outer rows.

fields.Text: The cost based optimizer approach, choosing plans by estimated cost and join order, was described for IBM's {{c1::System R}} by Selinger et al. in 1979.
fields.Hint: An IBM research prototype that shaped SQL.
fields.Fact: The paper introduced the idea of interesting orders when choosing join plans.
fields.Source: Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System, Selinger et al., 1979 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/582095.582099)

fields.Text: {{c1::Atomicity}} means a transaction's changes take effect entirely or not at all.
fields.Fact: After a crash, recovery undoes changes from transactions that never committed.
fields.Source: Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery, T. Haerder and A. Reuter, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/289.291)

fields.Text: In ACID, {{c1::consistency}} means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints.
fields.Hint: Not the same word as in CAP.
fields.Fact: The C in CAP refers to linearizability, a different concept.
fields.Source: Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery, T. Haerder and A. Reuter, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/289.291)

fields.Text: {{c1::Isolation}} means concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate effects, to a degree set by the isolation level.
fields.Fact: Full isolation corresponds to serializability.
fields.Source: Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery, T. Haerder and A. Reuter, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/289.291)

fields.Text: {{c1::Durability}} means once a transaction commits, its effects survive crashes.
fields.Fact: Most databases achieve this by flushing a log to stable storage before acknowledging commit.
fields.Source: Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery, T. Haerder and A. Reuter, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/289.291)

fields.Question: Which two authors coined the acronym ACID in 1983?
fields.Aliases:
Härder and Reuter
Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter
Reuter and Haerder
fields.Fact: The term appeared in their paper on transaction oriented database recovery.
fields.Source: Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery, T. Haerder and A. Reuter, 1983 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/289.291)

fields.Question: What anomaly occurs when a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed?
fields.Hint: The data might later be rolled back.
fields.Fact: PostgreSQL never allows dirty reads, even at READ UNCOMMITTED.

fields.Question: What anomaly occurs when a transaction reads the same row twice and sees different values because another transaction committed in between?
fields.Fact: REPEATABLE READ is named after preventing exactly this.

fields.Question: What anomaly occurs when rerunning a query with the same search condition returns a different set of rows due to another committed transaction?
fields.Fact: The ANSI standard allows it at REPEATABLE READ, but PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ prevents it.

fields.Question: What anomaly occurs when two transactions read a value, both modify it, and one write silently overwrites the other?
fields.Hint: A classic read modify write race.
fields.Fact: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or an atomic UPDATE x = x + 1 prevents it.
fields.Source: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, Berenson et al., 1995 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)

fields.Question: Which anomaly lets two transactions read overlapping data, write disjoint rows, and together break an invariant, even under snapshot isolation?
fields.Hint: The classic example is two doctors both going off call.
fields.Fact: Berenson et al. described it while showing snapshot isolation is weaker than serializable.
fields.Source: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, Berenson et al., 1995 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)

fields.Question: What is PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level?
fields.Hint: Each statement sees a fresh snapshot.
fields.Fact: In PostgreSQL, READ UNCOMMITTED behaves the same as READ COMMITTED.

fields.Question: What is the default isolation level of MySQL's InnoDB engine?
fields.Fact: InnoDB uses next key locks at this level to limit phantoms for locking reads.
fields.Source: MySQL Reference Manual: Transaction Isolation Levels (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html)

fields.Question: Which ANSI SQL isolation level is the strongest?
fields.Hint: Results equal some one at a time order.
fields.Fact: It is the only level the standard says forbids all three named phenomena.

fields.Question: Which ANSI SQL isolation level is the weakest and permits dirty reads?
fields.Hint: Its name says what it can see.
fields.Fact: Many engines, including PostgreSQL, quietly treat it as something stronger.

fields.Text: In PostgreSQL, a transaction at {{c1::Repeatable Read}} sees a snapshot taken at the start of its first statement, not of each statement.
fields.Fact: Updating a row another transaction has changed since the snapshot raises a serialization failure.

fields.Text: {{c1::Snapshot isolation}} lets each transaction read from a consistent snapshot and aborts one of two concurrent writers to the same row.
fields.Hint: Formalized by Berenson et al. in 1995.
fields.Fact: It prevents lost updates and the ANSI phantom anomaly but still allows write skew.
fields.Source: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, Berenson et al., 1995 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)

fields.Text: Since 9.1, PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using {{c1::Serializable Snapshot Isolation}}, which tracks read write dependencies and aborts transactions that could form an anomaly.
fields.Hint: Built on top of snapshot isolation.
fields.Fact: SSI was proposed by Cahill, Röhm and Fekete in 2008.
fields.Source: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL, D. Ports and K. Grittner, 2012 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4179)

fields.Fact: Applications using it must be ready to retry on serialization failures.
fields.Source: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL, D. Ports and K. Grittner, 2012 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4179)

fields.Question: What SQLSTATE does PostgreSQL return for a serialization failure that the client should retry?
fields.Fact: The PostgreSQL docs recommend retrying the whole transaction on this error.

fields.Text: {{c1::Multiversion concurrency control}} keeps multiple versions of rows so readers see a snapshot and do not block writers.
fields.Fact: In PostgreSQL, reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading under MVCC.

fields.Aliases:
multiversion concurrency control
multi-version concurrency control
fields.Fact: PostgreSQL, Oracle and InnoDB all use forms of it.

fields.Text: {{c1::Two phase locking}} acquires locks in a growing phase and releases them in a shrinking phase, which guarantees serializability.
fields.Hint: No new lock after the first release.
fields.Fact: Strict 2PL holds write locks until commit to avoid cascading aborts.
fields.Source: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, Berenson et al., 1995 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)

fields.Fact: Not to be confused with 2PC, which coordinates distributed commits.
fields.Source: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, Berenson et al., 1995 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0701157)

fields.Fact: PostgreSQL exposes it as PREPARE TRANSACTION and COMMIT PREPARED.

fields.Text: Two {{c1::shared}} locks on the same item are compatible, but an {{c2::exclusive}} lock conflicts with every other lock on it.
fields.Fact: Lock compatibility matrices generalize this to many lock modes.

fields.Text: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 {{c1::FOR UPDATE}};
fields.Extra: Locks the selected rows until the transaction ends.
fields.Fact: Adding SKIP LOCKED makes it useful for job queues.

fields.Text: FOR UPDATE {{c1::SKIP LOCKED}} ignores rows already locked by others, a common way to build a work queue on PostgreSQL.
fields.Hint: Workers do not wait for each other.
fields.Fact: NOWAIT is the alternative that raises an error instead of skipping.

fields.Text: A {{c1::deadlock}} occurs when transactions wait on each other's locks in a cycle; PostgreSQL detects it and aborts one of them.
fields.Hint: A cycle in the wait for graph.
fields.Fact: Acquiring locks in a consistent order across transactions prevents most deadlocks.

fields.Question: What is PostgreSQL's default deadlock_timeout?
fields.Hint: The wait before running the detector.
fields.Fact: The check is deferred because deadlock detection is relatively expensive.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL table lock mode conflicts with every other mode, including plain SELECT?
fields.Fact: Many ALTER TABLE forms take this lock, so they can block reads on a busy table.

fields.Text: With {{c1::write-ahead logging}}, changes are recorded in a log that is flushed to durable storage before the data pages are written.
fields.Fact: It lets a database recover after a crash by replaying the log.

fields.Aliases:
write-ahead logging
write ahead log
write-ahead log
fields.Fact: PostgreSQL stores WAL in the pg_wal directory.

fields.Text: A {{c1::checkpoint}} flushes dirty data pages so older WAL is no longer needed for crash recovery.
fields.Fact: In PostgreSQL, checkpoint_timeout defaults to 5 minutes.

fields.Text: The {{c1::ARIES}} recovery algorithm uses three passes after a crash: analysis, redo, and undo.
fields.Fact: ARIES redoes history, including changes of losing transactions, before undoing them.
fields.Source: ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method, C. Mohan et al., 1992 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/128765.128770)

fields.Text: Setting PostgreSQL's {{c1::synchronous_commit}} = off can lose the last few transactions on crash but never corrupts the database.
fields.Fact: Unlike fsync = off, it does not risk inconsistency, only recent commits.

fields.Text: In {{c1::single leader}} replication, all writes go to one node, which streams changes to read only followers.
fields.Fact: Followers can serve reads, but they may lag behind the leader.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)

fields.Text: {{c1::Multi-leader}} replication accepts writes on several nodes, so it must resolve conflicting concurrent writes.
fields.Fact: Last write wins is a simple but lossy conflict resolution strategy.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)

fields.Text: In {{c1::leaderless}} replication, as in Dynamo, clients write to and read from several replicas directly.
fields.Fact: Cassandra and Riak follow this Dynamo style design.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: With N replicas, reads from R nodes and writes to W nodes overlap on at least one node when {{c1::R + W > N}}.
fields.Fact: Dynamo described this as a quorum like system with configurable N, R and W.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: With {{c1::asynchronous}} replication, the primary acknowledges commits before standbys confirm, so failover can lose recent transactions.
fields.Fact: The lost window is bounded by replication lag.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)

fields.Text: With {{c1::synchronous}} replication, a commit waits until a standby confirms it has the WAL.
fields.Fact: It adds at least one network round trip to every commit.

fields.Text: PostgreSQL {{c1::streaming replication}} ships WAL records to standbys, which replay them to stay a physical copy of the primary.
fields.Fact: Physical standbys must run the same major PostgreSQL version as the primary.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html)

fields.Text: PostgreSQL {{c1::logical replication}} uses publications and subscriptions to replicate row changes for chosen tables.
fields.Fact: Because it is row based, it can replicate between different major versions.

fields.Text: {{c1::Raft}} is a consensus algorithm with leader election and log replication, designed to be easier to understand than Paxos.
fields.Fact: etcd and CockroachDB both build on Raft.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, D. Ongaro and J. Ousterhout, 2014 (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: How many node failures can a 5 node Raft cluster tolerate while still making progress?
fields.Fact: In general, 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, D. Ongaro and J. Ousterhout, 2014 (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Text: {{c1::Sharding}} splits a dataset horizontally across multiple machines, each holding a subset of rows.
fields.Fact: Cross shard joins and transactions are usually much more expensive than local ones.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data, Chang et al., 2006 (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Text: {{c1::Hash partitioning}} spreads keys evenly but makes range queries touch every partition.
fields.Fact: Cassandra's default partitioner hashes keys with Murmur3.

fields.Text: {{c1::Range partitioning}} keeps adjacent keys together, enabling efficient range scans but risking hot spots on sequential keys.
fields.Hint: Bigtable splits tables into tablets this way.
fields.Fact: Timestamp keys are a classic source of a hot last partition.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data, Chang et al., 2006 (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Text: {{c1::Consistent hashing}} maps keys and nodes onto a ring, so adding a node moves only about 1/n of the keys.
fields.Fact: Dynamo used virtual nodes on the ring to balance load across machines.
fields.Source:
Consistent Hashing and Random Trees, Karger et al., 1997 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/258533.258660)
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: PostgreSQL declarative partitioning supports {{c1::range}}, {{c2::list}} and {{c3::hash}} partitioning.
fields.Fact: Declarative partitioning arrived in PostgreSQL 10; hash partitioning was added in 11.

fields.Text: The CAP theorem says that during a network {{c1::partition}}, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.
fields.Fact: Gilbert and Lynch proved the formal version in 2002.
fields.Source: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services, S. Gilbert and N. Lynch, 2002 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/564585.564601)

fields.Question: Who presented the CAP conjecture in a 2000 PODC keynote?
fields.Fact: Gilbert and Lynch turned the conjecture into a proven theorem in 2002.
fields.Source: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services, S. Gilbert and N. Lynch, 2002 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/564585.564601)

fields.Text: PACELC says: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose {{c1::Latency}} or Consistency.
fields.Hint: The tradeoff that exists even without failures.
fields.Fact: Daniel Abadi proposed PACELC to capture the normal operation tradeoff CAP ignores.
fields.Source: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design, D. Abadi, 2012 (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)

fields.Question: Who proposed the PACELC formulation?
fields.Hint: A database researcher, then at Yale.
fields.Fact: His 2012 IEEE Computer article classified systems like Dynamo and PNUTS.
fields.Source: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design, D. Abadi, 2012 (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)

fields.Question: Under PACELC, Abadi classifies default Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak as which type?
fields.Fact: Abadi noted that fully ACID systems like VoltDB are PC/EC.
fields.Source: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design, D. Abadi, 2012 (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)

fields.Question: Under PACELC, Abadi classifies fully ACID systems such as VoltDB as which type?
fields.Fact: He grouped Megastore with them as well.
fields.Source: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design, D. Abadi, 2012 (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)

fields.Text: {{c1::Eventual consistency}} guarantees that if no new updates are made, all replicas eventually converge to the same value.
fields.Fact: Amazon's Dynamo is a well known example of an eventually consistent store.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: {{c1::Linearizability}} requires every operation to appear to take effect atomically at some point between its start and end, respecting real time order.
fields.Hint: The strongest single object consistency model.
fields.Fact: It is what CAP means by consistency.
fields.Source: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services, S. Gilbert and N. Lynch, 2002 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/564585.564601)

fields.Text: Dynamo used {{c1::vector clocks}} to detect concurrent conflicting versions of an object.
fields.Hint: A list of counters, one per node.
fields.Fact: Conflicting versions were returned to the client to reconcile, as in the shopping cart example.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: With {{c1::hinted handoff}}, a node temporarily accepts writes meant for an unreachable replica and forwards them when it returns.
fields.Fact: This keeps writes available during temporary failures.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: A {{c1::key-value}} store maps opaque keys to values and offers get and put by key.
fields.Fact: Amazon's Dynamo paper described one of the most influential designs.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, DeCandia et al., 2007 (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: A {{c1::document}} store keeps self describing records, such as JSON like objects, that can be queried by their fields.
fields.Fact: MongoDB stores documents in BSON, a binary JSON like format.

fields.Text: A {{c1::wide-column}} store, like Bigtable or Cassandra, organizes data by row key and column families, with sparse columns.
fields.Fact: Bigtable is a sparse, distributed, persistent multidimensional sorted map.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data, Chang et al., 2006 (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Text: A {{c1::graph}} database stores nodes and relationships as first class objects, making multi hop traversals cheap.
fields.Fact: Neo4j's query language Cypher uses ASCII art like (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) patterns.

fields.Question: MongoDB belongs to which NoSQL family?
fields.Fact: A MongoDB document is limited to 16 MB in BSON.

fields.Question: Apache Cassandra belongs to which NoSQL family?
fields.Hint: It combines Dynamo distribution with a Bigtable like data model.
fields.Fact: Cassandra was originally developed at Facebook.

fields.Question: Neo4j belongs to which NoSQL family?
fields.Fact: Cypher was originally created by Neo4j.

fields.Question: Redis is primarily described as which kind of data store?
fields.Aliases:
key-value
key value
in-memory data structure store
fields.Fact: Redis values can be strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams and more.

fields.Question: What binary serialization format does MongoDB use to store documents?
fields.Fact: BSON adds types JSON lacks, such as dates and binary data.

fields.Question: What is the name of Neo4j's declarative graph query language?
fields.Hint: It shares its name with a secret code.
fields.Fact: Its MATCH clause describes graph patterns to find.

fields.Text: A {{c1::log-structured merge tree}} buffers writes in memory and flushes them as immutable sorted files that are later merged.
fields.Fact: LSM trees power Cassandra, RocksDB and LevelDB.
fields.Source: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree), O'Neil et al., 1996 (https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf)

fields.Aliases:
log structured merge tree
log-structured merge-tree
fields.Fact: O'Neil et al. described it in 1996.
fields.Source: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree), O'Neil et al., 1996 (https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf)

fields.Text: In Bigtable style storage, recent writes go to an in memory {{c1::memtable}}, which is flushed to an immutable {{c2::SSTable}} on disk.
fields.Fact: A commit log is written first so the memtable can be rebuilt after a crash.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data, Chang et al., 2006 (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Text: LSM based stores keep a {{c1::Bloom filter}} per SSTable to skip files that definitely lack a key.
fields.Fact: Bigtable lets clients enable Bloom filters per locality group to cut disk reads.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data, Chang et al., 2006 (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Text: Compared with a B-tree, an LSM tree typically favors {{c1::writes}}, at the cost of extra read work and background compaction.
fields.Hint: Sequential flushes versus in place updates.
fields.Fact: B-trees update pages in place, which means random writes.
fields.Source: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree), O'Neil et al., 1996 (https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf)

fields.Question: What is PostgreSQL's default page (block) size?
fields.Hint: A power of two in kilobytes.
fields.Fact: It can only be changed when compiling PostgreSQL.

fields.Text: PostgreSQL's {{c1::VACUUM}} reclaims space from dead row versions left behind by updates and deletes.
fields.Fact: Autovacuum runs it automatically based on how many rows have changed.

fields.Text: PostgreSQL transaction IDs are {{c1::32}} bits, so tables must be vacuumed regularly to freeze old rows and avoid wraparound.
fields.Fact: If wraparound gets too close, PostgreSQL refuses new transactions to protect data.

fields.Text: PostgreSQL stores large field values out of line using {{c1::TOAST}}, compressing and splitting them into chunks.
fields.Hint: Its name is a breakfast pun.
fields.Fact: TOAST usually triggers when a row exceeds about 2 kB.

fields.Aliases:
the oversized-attribute storage technique
oversized attribute storage technique
fields.Fact: The docs call it "the best thing since sliced bread".

fields.Text: A {{c1::heap-only tuple}} (HOT) update avoids new index entries when no indexed column changes and the new version fits on the same page.
fields.Hint: Lowering fillfactor makes it more likely.
fields.Fact: HOT updates reduce index bloat from frequent updates.
HOT was introduced in PostgreSQL 8.3.

fields.Question: Which PostgreSQL type stores JSON in a decomposed binary form that supports GIN indexing?
fields.Hint: The other one stores the exact input text.
fields.Fact: jsonb does not preserve key order or duplicate keys; json does.

fields.Text:
CREATE TABLE t (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS {{c1::IDENTITY}} PRIMARY KEY
);
fields.Extra: The SQL standard alternative to serial.
fields.Hint: Standard syntax for auto generated keys.
fields.Fact: Identity columns were added in PostgreSQL 10.

fields.Question: PostgreSQL descends from which research project at UC Berkeley led by Michael Stonebraker?
fields.Fact: The name was changed to PostgreSQL in 1996 to reflect its SQL support.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL Documentation: A Brief History of PostgreSQL (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/history.html)

fields.Question: Can CREATE TABLE be rolled back inside a PostgreSQL transaction?
fields.Hint: PostgreSQL treats most DDL as transactional.
fields.Fact: Exceptions include CREATE DATABASE and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

fields.Question: What licensing status does SQLite's source code have?
fields.Fact: The SQLite authors offer a purchased license for organizations that require one.

fields.Question: Which PRAGMA switches an SQLite database to write-ahead logging?
fields.Fact: WAL mode persists across connections once set.

fields.Text: In SQLite WAL mode, readers do not block the writer and the writer does not block readers, but there can still be only {{c1::one writer}} at a time.
fields.Hint: Concurrency is limited on one side.
fields.Fact: WAL mode requires all processes to be on the same host, since it uses shared memory.

fields.Question: Unless changed, what journaling approach does SQLite use for transactions?
fields.Fact: WAL mode was added in SQLite 3.7.0 in 2010.
fields.Source:
SQLite: Write-Ahead Logging (https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)
SQLite: PRAGMA Statements (https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html)

fields.Text: SQLite uses dynamic typing: a column has a type {{c1::affinity}}, and the value itself carries its storage class.
fields.Fact: A column declared INTEGER can still hold a text value that cannot be converted.

fields.Question: SQLite has five storage classes: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, BLOB, and which other one?
fields.Fact: Booleans are stored as integers 0 and 1.

fields.Text: SQLite {{c1::STRICT}} tables, added in 3.37.0, enforce declared column types.
fields.Hint: A keyword at the end of CREATE TABLE.
fields.Fact: STRICT tables only allow types INT, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and ANY.

fields.Text: In SQLite, a column declared {{c1::INTEGER PRIMARY KEY}} becomes an alias for the rowid.
fields.Fact: Declaring INT PRIMARY KEY instead does not create the alias.
fields.Source: SQLite: CREATE TABLE, ROWIDs and the INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (https://www.sqlite.org/lang_createtable.html#rowid)

fields.Text: SQLite foreign key enforcement is off by default and must be enabled per connection with PRAGMA {{c1::foreign_keys}} = ON.
fields.Hint: A pragma named after the feature.
fields.Fact: This default exists for backward compatibility.

fields.Text: A SQLite {{c1::WITHOUT ROWID}} table stores rows in a clustered B-tree keyed by its primary key.
fields.Fact: Such tables must have a PRIMARY KEY.

fields.Question: Which SQLite BEGIN variant takes the write lock at the start of the transaction instead of on the first write?
fields.Fact: Starting write transactions this way avoids some SQLITE_BUSY upgrade failures.

fields.Question: What is SQLite's default page size in bytes for new databases since version 3.12.0?
fields.Hint: Matches many file system block sizes.
fields.Fact: Page size must be a power of two between 512 and 65536.

fields.Question: Which SQLite command prefix shows the high level query plan for a statement?
fields.Fact: Plain EXPLAIN in SQLite lists virtual machine opcodes rather than a readable plan.
